newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Broaddus unsure if U.S. rates high enough.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Broaddus unsure if U.S. rates high enough.

text.p: Richmond Federal Reserve Bank President Alfred Broaddus said Wednesday he saw signs that economic growth was slowing from it's recent rapid pace.
But he told the Washington Association of Money Managers that he did not know if interest rates were high enough to moderate growth to a long-term, sustainable level.
The economy on average has grown at an annualized pace of close to five percent over the last two quarters, a rate that Broaddus said probably cannot be sustained without fanning inflation.
"The economy is already operating at a very high level," Broaddus said. "There is not a lot of headroom."
Private economists on average expect solid economic growth this year of about three percent and continued tight labor markets, but no big outbreak of inflation.

Broaddus said he saw no reason why that forecast could not turn out to be correct. But he said that there were more upside risks that growth would be faster and inflation higher than the forecast than downside risks of economic slowdown.
"The risk is greater on the upside," he said.
However, Broaddus noted that consumer spending has softened a bit in March and April. That suggests that the economy may be slowing, which might be a healthy development, he said.
Price pressures have remained "remarkably subdued," but that may be due to temporary factors, such as worker fear of job loss, whose influence could wane.
The strong dollar has also helped to contain inflation by holding down import prices and increasing competition from overseas, he said.
But he added, "Dollar strength cannot be counted on indefinitely," noting that the U.S. currency has recently eased.
Broaddus stressed the importance of the Fed following what he called a forward-looking monetary policy with an ultimate goal of price stability.
"It's vitally important we stay ahead of the inflation curve, especially now (that the economy is running at a high level)," he said.
Provided the Fed retains its vigilance against inflation, Broaddus said he saw no reason not to expect the U.S. economic expansion to continue through 1998 and beyond.
Noting that U.S. long-term interest rates have eased recently, Broaddus voiced hopes that that was a sign of confidence in the Fed's anti-inflation stance.
Broaddus declined to say why the Fed opted to leave interest rates unchanged at its meeting last month.
He depicted the central bank's 0.25 percentage point rate increase in March as a response to a stronger economy and heightened demand for credit.
"It's not unreasonable to expect the price of credit to rise (in that type of situation)," he said.
Responding to a question, Broaddus said that he was optimistic that Europe would eventually succeed in forging a single currency.
"I don't think it's going to be sidetracked permanently ... I'm optimistic in the long run," he said.

Europe is trying to launch monetary union in 1999, but Broaddus said that the left's triumph in recent French elections and the row in Germany over the revaluation of its gold reserves raised questions about the timing of monetary union.
"It's a lot dicier situation," he said. "We've hit a pretty big bump."
